Cell-type perturbation in MASH vs healthy liver

Author

Richard Ahn, PhD

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(Seurat)
  library(Matrix)
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(patchwork)
  library(speckle)     # propeller: donor-level differential abundance
  library(DESeq2)      # pseudobulk differential expression

  library(knitr)
})

set.seed(1234)

# Format p-values for inline prose. signif() alone yields values like 1.3e-07,
# which the inline hook renders as broken superscript markup.
fmt_p <- function(x) {
  x <- unname(x[1])
  if (is.na(x)) return("NA")
  if (x < 1e-3) formatC(x, format = "e", digits = 1) else formatC(signif(x, 2), format = "g")
}

CACHE_DIR <- "cache"
dir.create(CACHE_DIR, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
cache_path <- function(name) file.path(CACHE_DIR, name)

# Compute-or-load guard. Expensive steps that touch the full object write a
# small intermediate to cache/ and reuse it on later renders. Deleting cache/
# forces a full cold run, so the document stays reproducible from the raw data.
cached <- function(name, expr) {
  p <- cache_path(name)
  if (file.exists(p)) return(readRDS(p))
  x <- force(expr)
  saveRDS(x, p)
  x
}

# COL1A1 counts for every nucleus, needed in two separate sections. Wrapped in a
# function so neither section depends on the other having run first.
col1a1_counts <- function() cached("col1a1_distribution.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  as.vector(as.matrix(open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")["COL1A1", ]))
})

Introduction

The prompt is to take a MASH scRNA-seq or snRNA-seq dataset and highlight which cell types are most perturbed and how relative to healthy liver. I think “most perturbed” carries two distinct meanings:

  1. Differential abundance. Which cell types change in proportion between MASH and control. A cell type can be strongly perturbed here while its surviving cells look transcriptionally ordinary.
  2. Within-cell-type differential expression. How the cells of a given type are transcriptionally rewired in disease. A cell type can hold steady in proportion while its program shifts substantially.

These are measured separately below and only combined at the end, in a ranked table that answers the prompt on both axes.

The cohort is staged rather than binary: healthy control, isolated steatosis (MASL), early MASH and advanced MASH. The primary comparison is the clean case-control contrast of control against MASH, with MASL held out so that cases with steatosis but no steatohepatitis do not dilute it. MASL is then put back to work in two secondary views: an ordered trend across all four stages, and stage-adjacent contrasts that localize where along the progression each cell type actually changes. A cell type that shifts only between early and advanced MASH is telling a different story from one that shifts at the onset of steatosis, and the two-group contrast alone cannot distinguish them.

I made the decision to run analyses at the donor level, not the cell level. A dataset of a quarter of a million nuclei from 48 people now carries 48 independent observations, not 250,000. Abundance is therefore tested on donor-level proportions, and expression on donor-level pseudobulk.

I used Claude Code Opus 5 for this report.

Executive summary

Hepatocytes are the most perturbed cell type, and the only one perturbed on both axes. They lose more than half their share of nuclei across the progression from control to MASH, and those nuclei carry more differentially expressed genes than any other cell type by a wide margin. The program is coherent: p53 and growth arrest up, differentiated metabolic function down, with bile acid, xenobiotic and fatty acid metabolism all depleted. The compositional result independently reproduces the source paper’s headline.

Endothelial cells do not change in abundance at all, yet carry the second-largest expression program in the dataset, and its content is inflammatory activation. T cells expand several-fold in number while changing their expression program comparatively little.

Macrophages change identity rather than number, switching from the resident Kupffer program to a lipid-handling, scar-associated one. This is the most mechanistically specific result here, and it reproduces the macrophage arm of the fibrotic niche described in cirrhosis by Ramachandran et al., in a cohort that has not reached cirrhosis.

Two results required correcting the deposited annotation rather than trusting it. A subcluster labeled as inactivated stellate cells is vascular mural tissue, which inverts the apparent direction of the stellate contractile program when the label is aggregated. And stellate abundance appears unchanged in the two-group contrast because it is not monotonic: the compartment expands only at advanced fibrosis, which a control-versus-MASH comparison cancels out.

What this dataset cannot answer. It does not contain collagen-producing myofibroblasts, and two of the three scar-associated populations from the reference cirrhosis atlas are absent while the one not embedded in scar replicates cleanly. I think the explanation is that needle-core biopsy tissue does not recover cells resident in dense matrix. The consequence is nothing here bears on myofibroblast biology in either direction, and the flat collagen result is a sampling limit rather than evidence against fibrogenesis.

Implications for therapeutics are limited to target engageability. The receptors for thyromimetic, FXR and PPAR-alpha agonism are well expressed in the cell types those drugs act on, and the programs they regulate are among the things disease has disturbed. GLP-1 and GIP receptors are not expressed in this tissue, so a liver atlas is the wrong instrument for those agents. However, the glucagon arm of a dual agonist is the exception, with a direct and measurable hepatocyte target. Anti-fibrotic targets cannot be assessed, for the sampling reason above. None of this speaks to potential efficacy.

Data provenance

Single-nucleus RNA-seq of 48 human liver biopsies spanning the MASLD spectrum, from Hong et al., Nature Genetics 2025. Raw data are deposited under GEO GSE289173 (BioProject PRJNA1221860); the processed Seurat object analyzed here is distributed via Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.14586466, CC-BY 4.0).

Why this dataset

Several candidate datasets were considered before settling on this one (see table below). I chose the Hong et al. dataset because it is snRNA-seq, includes MASH and control samples from human liver biopsies, has a sufficient number of donors and nuclei, and, decisively, because its processed data was verified as downloadable rather than merely deposited.

# Dataset (accession) Human Liver biopsy Indication sc / sn Atlas Download verified?
1 sc-eQTL MASH, Hong 2025 (GSE289173 / Zenodo 14586466) Yes Yes MASH + control sn No (cohort) Yes — processed Seurat v4 on Zenodo, CC-BY, 6.6 GB, opened and confirmed
2 EphB2 NASH transition, Xiao 2023 (GSE189600) Yes (+ mouse) Yes NAFL→NASH sn (+ snATAC) No Strongly — independently re-downloaded from GEO by ≥3 later papers
3 Spatial multi-omics MASLD atlas, NatGen 2025 (s41588-025-02407-8) Yes Yes control / MASL / MASH both Yes Not yet — accession not confirmed
4 Human HSC multi-omics, J Hepatol 2024 (S0168-8278(24)02667-9) Yes Yes normal / MASL / MASH sn (+ snATAC) No (HSC-only) Not yet — accession not confirmed
5 Human snRNA-seq MASH (GSE212837) Yes Yes MASH sn No Deposited + reused; file listing not opened
6 Human scRNA-seq MASH (GSE189175) Yes Yes MASH sc No Deposited + reused; file listing not opened
— Copenhagen NASH, Fred 2022 Yes Yes NASH sc No Excluded — no raw data released, no healthy controls

The Hong et al. study is primarily a single-cell eQTL analysis, and its headline result is a hepatocyte maladaptation signal at EFHD1/FOXO1. The cell-type perturbation question asked here is described in that paper but not developed in depth, and its differential expression was run cell-level with Seurat FindMarkers. The contribution of this report is to answer the perturbation question directly, with donor-level replication on both axes.

The downloadable object was built with Cellranger, Cellbender for ambient RNA, DoubletFinder for doublets, Liger for integration and Seurat for clustering. Liger was not an arbitrary choice: the authors benchmarked it against FastMNN, Harmony, CCA and RPCA on kBET acceptance rate and selected it on that basis. Normalization was done with scran and batchelor rather than Seurat’s log-normalization. This analysis reuses that object and its integration as-is, and validates the annotations rather than re-deriving them.

Cohort, contrasts and marker panels

The Zenodo deposit ships tidied metadata: seven columns, with disease stage already in current MASLD/MASH nomenclature rather than the pre-2023 NAFLD terms used in the authors’ analysis scripts. No remapping is needed.

Two annotation columns are supplied. Cell_type_broad gives 14 labels; Cell_type_detailed gives 19, and nests cleanly inside the broad column. Only two lineages subdivide, and both subdivide along exactly the axis MASH acts on: hepatocytes split by zonation, stellate cells by activation state. That is used below, after the primary analysis, to ask where within a lineage the perturbation sits.

Code 
# Metadata columns, confirmed against the object rather than assumed.
COL_DONOR    <- "DonorID"
COL_STAGE    <- "Disease_group"
COL_CT_BROAD <- "Cell_type_broad"
COL_CT_FINE  <- "Cell_type_detailed"

# Disease stage, in the order of progression.
STAGE_LEVELS <- c("control", "MASL", "eMASH", "aMASH")
STAGE_LABELS <- c(control = "No-MASLD", MASL = "MASL",
                  eMASH = "eMASH", aMASH = "aMASH")

# Primary contrast is two-group. MASL is the intermediate stage and is held out
# of it, so the headline case-control comparison is not diluted by cases that
# have steatosis without steatohepatitis. MASL is not discarded: it carries the
# ordered trend analysis and the stage-adjacent contrasts defined below.
CONDITION_MAP <- c(control = "Control", MASL = NA,
                   eMASH = "MASH", aMASH = "MASH")
CONDITION_LEVELS <- c("Control", "MASH")

# Secondary stage-wise contrasts, run after the primary. Each is a step along
# the progression, which localizes where in the disease course a cell type
# changes rather than only whether it differs at the endpoint.
STAGE_CONTRASTS <- list(
  c("control", "MASL"),   # onset of steatosis
  c("MASL",    "eMASH"),  # steatosis to steatohepatitis
  c("control", "eMASH"),  # control to early MASH
  c("eMASH",   "aMASH"),  # early to advanced fibrosis
  c("control", "aMASH")   # full span, largest expected effect
)

# Thresholds for calling a gene differentially expressed. Significance alone
# admits very small effects when donor numbers are adequate, so an effect-size
# floor is applied alongside it. Both are stated wherever counts are reported.
FDR_CUTOFF <- 0.05
LFC_CUTOFF <- 0.25

# Applied to every DESeq2 result table in this report.
is_de <- function(r) {
  !is.na(r$padj) & r$padj < FDR_CUTOFF & abs(r$log2FoldChange) >= LFC_CUTOFF
}
DE_RULE <- paste0("FDR < ", FDR_CUTOFF, " and |log2FC| >= ", LFC_CUTOFF)

# Not cell types. Per the source paper's supplementary methods, "Unidentified"
# marks cells whose substate assignment disagreed between the joint and the
# disease-stratified subclustering. Excluded from every analysis below.
DROP_LABELS <- c("Suspected_doublet", "Unidentified")

# Canonical human liver markers, used to verify the shipped annotations before
# any claim is built on them.
LIVER_MARKERS <- list(
  Hepatocyte    = c("ALB", "APOA1", "TTR", "CYP2E1", "HNF4A", "ASGR1"),
  Cholangiocyte = c("KRT19", "KRT7", "EPCAM", "SOX9", "CFTR"),
  Stellate      = c("COL1A1", "COL3A1", "DCN", "PDGFRB", "RGS5"),
  Endothelial   = c("PECAM1", "VWF", "CLEC4G", "STAB2", "LYVE1"),
  Kupffer_Mac   = c("CD68", "MARCO", "VSIG4", "C1QA", "CD5L"),
  Scar_Mac      = c("TREM2", "CD9", "GPNMB", "SPP1", "LYZ"),
  T_cell        = c("CD3D", "CD3E", "CD8A", "IL7R"),
  NK            = c("NKG7", "GNLY", "KLRD1"),
  B_Plasma      = c("CD79A", "MS4A1", "MZB1", "IGHG1")
)

# programs the differential expression results are checked against. These are
# recovered from the data, not asserted; they exist here to make the check
# explicit rather than post hoc.
MASH_PROGRAMS <- list(
  HSC_activation      = c("COL1A1", "COL3A1", "ACTA2", "TIMP1", "TAGLN"),
  Scar_macrophage     = c("TREM2", "CD9", "GPNMB", "SPP1"),
  Kupffer_homeostatic = c("MARCO", "VSIG4", "CD5L", "CLEC4F"),
  LSEC_identity       = c("CLEC4G", "STAB2", "LYVE1", "OIT3"),
  Ductular_reaction   = c("KRT19", "KRT7", "SOX9", "EPCAM")
)

Loading the object

The deposited object is Seurat v4 and occupies roughly 14 GB once loaded, which leaves no headroom on a 16 GB machine. That shapes the code below, especially the decision to run on-disk using BPCells.

Everything expensive runs once, writes a compact intermediate to cache/, and is reused afterwards. Counts are additionally written to an on-disk BPCells matrix, so per-cell-type aggregation streams from disk instead of holding a 24,615 x 249,233 sparse matrix in RAM. Deleting cache/ and bpcells_counts/ forces a full recomputation from the deposited file.

Code 
RDS <- "data/unzipped/Zenodo/processed_seurat_object/MASLD_snRNA_seq_seurat_v4.rds"

if (!file.exists(cache_path("meta.rds")) || !dir.exists("bpcells_counts")) {
  library(BPCells)
  mem.maxVSize(vsize = 64000)          # allow the load to spill past physical RAM
  obj <- readRDS(RDS)
  rna <- obj@assays$RNA

  saveRDS(obj@meta.data, cache_path("meta.rds"))
  saveRDS(list(dim = dim(obj), reductions = names(obj@reductions),
               genes = rownames(rna), seurat_ver = as.character(obj@version)),
          cache_path("obj_info.rds"))
  for (rd in names(obj@reductions)) {
    e <- obj@reductions[[rd]]@cell.embeddings
    saveRDS(e[, 1:min(3, ncol(e))], cache_path(paste0("emb_", rd, ".rds")))
  }

  cnt <- rna@counts                     # raw integer counts, required for pseudobulk
  rm(obj, rna); gc()
  BPCells::write_matrix_dir(cnt, dir = "bpcells_counts", compress = TRUE)
  rm(cnt); gc()
}

md   <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
info <- readRDS(cache_path("obj_info.rds"))

md$stage     <- factor(md[[COL_STAGE]], levels = STAGE_LEVELS,
                       labels = STAGE_LABELS[STAGE_LEVELS])
md$condition <- factor(unname(CONDITION_MAP[as.character(md[[COL_STAGE]])]),
                       levels = CONDITION_LEVELS)

# Technical labels are not cell types and are excluded from every analysis.
n_dropped <- sum(md[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS)
md <- md[!md[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS, ]

The object holds 249,233 nuclei and 24,615 genes, integrated with Liger (reductions: iNMF_raw, iNMF, umap). Dropping Suspected_doublet and Unidentified removes 9,323 nuclei, leaving 239,910 for analysis.

Cohort

Code 
donors <- unique(md[, c(COL_DONOR, "stage", "condition")])
names(donors)[1] <- "donor"

cohort <- as.data.frame(table(Stage = donors$stage), responseName = "Donors")
cohort$Nuclei <- as.integer(table(factor(md$stage, levels = levels(donors$stage))))
cohort$`Median nuclei/donor` <- round(tapply(
  as.integer(table(md[[COL_DONOR]]))[donors$donor], donors$stage, median))
cohort$`Primary contrast` <- ifelse(
  is.na(CONDITION_MAP[STAGE_LEVELS]), "held out",
  as.character(CONDITION_MAP[STAGE_LEVELS]))
kable(cohort, caption = "Cohort by disease stage.")
Cohort by disease stage.
Stage Donors Nuclei Median nuclei/donor Primary contrast
No-MASLD 23 145769 NA Control
MASL 6 20481 NA held out
eMASH 9 22171 NA MASH
aMASH 10 51489 NA MASH

48 donors, distributed as No-MASLD n=23, MASL n=6, eMASH n=9, aMASH n=10. This reproduces the cohort reported in the source paper exactly.

Note that the stages are not balanced in nuclei: controls contribute 61% of nuclei but only 48% of donors. Pooling nuclei across donors would therefore weight the control group nearly twice as heavily as its donor count warrants, which is the first practical reason the analyses below operate on per-donor quantities.

One further detail matters for anyone reusing this object: donor identifiers do not encode disease stage. All 20 ctrl_* donors are controls, but three further controls are named FL*. Condition must be taken from Disease_group, never parsed from the donor name.

Code 
kable(table(`Donor name` = ifelse(grepl("^ctrl", donors$donor), "ctrl_*", "FL*"),
            Stage = donors$stage),
      caption = "Donor naming does not track disease stage.")

QC and study design checks

This is validation of a processed object, not re-derivation. The object has already been through Cellbender ambient-RNA removal and DoubletFinder. The question is whether anything about its quality differs systematically between conditions in a way that could masquerade as biology.

Code 
qc <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  md[, c("condition", "stage", "nCount_RNA", "nFeature_RNA", "percent.mt")],
  cols = c(nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, percent.mt),
  names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

ggplot(subset(qc, !is.na(condition)), aes(condition, value, fill = condition)) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.12, outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.3, fill = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#4C72B0", MASH = "#C44E52")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "value (log1p scale)") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "none")

For reference, the filters already applied by the source study, from its supplementary methods: singlets were retained on gene and read count with a per-donor threshold (count greater than 0.2 times that donor’s median) and genes expressed in fewer than 0.25% of cells in a donor were removed. At sample level, donors with a median below 200 genes per cell were excluded, along with one principal-component outlier and three samples failing genome-transcriptome concordance. Ambient RNA was removed with Cellbender and doublets with DoubletFinder before any of that. The checks below are therefore validation of an already-filtered object, not a second round of filtering.

percent.mt is essentially zero across the dataset (median 0, maximum 5%). That is the expected behavior for single-nucleus data, where mitochondrial transcripts are largely excluded with the cytoplasm. Mitochondrial filtering is not a meaningful QC axis here, and applying a conventional 5-10% threshold wouldn’t really be meaningful.

Depth differs modestly between conditions, which is worth knowing but is handled downstream: pseudobulk DE models library size explicitly through DESeq2’s size factors, and proportions are depth-invariant by construction.

Confounding

The design can only adjust for variables that vary within condition. Two checks decide the model formula.

Code 
# Does any donor contribute more than one condition?
per_donor <- table(md[[COL_DONOR]], md[[COL_STAGE]])
multi <- sum(rowSums(per_donor > 0) > 1)

meta_cols <- colnames(readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds")))

data.frame(
  Check = c("Metadata columns deposited",
            "Donors contributing >1 disease stage",
            "Batch / chemistry / center variable present"),
  Result = c(paste(meta_cols, collapse = ", "),
             as.character(multi),
             "none")
) |> kable(caption = "Design checks determining the DE formula.")
Design checks determining the DE formula.
Check Result
Metadata columns deposited DonorID, nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA, percent.mt, Cell_type_broad, Cell_type_detailed, Disease_group
Donors contributing >1 disease stage 0
Batch / chemistry / center variable present none

Every donor contributes exactly one disease stage, so donor is nested within condition. It therefore cannot enter the design: a donor term would absorb the between-donor variation that is the condition effect. This is a correctness constraint rather than a modeling preference.

The deposited metadata carries no batch, chemistry, sequencing-run or center variable. There is consequently nothing to adjust for, and the design stays ~ condition. This is a single-center Korean cohort, so the risk of hidden batch-condition confounding is lower than in a multi-dataset atlas.

Verifying annotations

Every claim below rests on the deposited labels, so they are checked against canonical liver markers before use. Expression is summarized per cell type from the on-disk counts: library-size normalized to 10,000, log1p transformed.

Code 
mk <- cached("markers_broad.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  keep <- !meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS
  ct   <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]])[keep])
  sub  <- mat[, which(keep)]
  normed <- log1p(multiply_cols(sub, 1e4 / colSums(sub)))
  genes  <- intersect(unique(unlist(LIVER_MARKERS)), rownames(mat))
  avg <- pseudobulk_matrix(normed[genes, ], cell_groups = ct, method = "mean")
  nz  <- pseudobulk_matrix(sub[genes, ],    cell_groups = ct, method = "nonzeros")
  pct <- sweep(nz, 2, as.integer(table(ct)), "/") * 100
  flat <- utils::stack(LIVER_MARKERS)
  data.frame(gene = rep(rownames(avg), ncol(avg)),
             cell_type = rep(colnames(avg), each = nrow(avg)),
             avg_exp = as.vector(avg), pct_exp = as.vector(pct),
             panel = as.character(flat$ind[match(rep(rownames(avg), ncol(avg)),
                                                 flat$values)]))
})

# Scale each gene across cell types so the dotplot shows specificity, not
# absolute abundance: a gene high everywhere is not evidence for any label.
mk <- mk |>
  group_by(gene) |>
  mutate(z = as.numeric(scale(avg_exp))) |>
  ungroup()
mk$gene      <- factor(mk$gene, levels = intersect(unlist(LIVER_MARKERS), mk$gene))
mk$cell_type <- factor(mk$cell_type, levels = rev(sort(unique(mk$cell_type))))

ggplot(mk, aes(gene, cell_type)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pct_exp, colour = z)) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "#3B4CC0", mid = "grey92", high = "#B40426",
                         midpoint = 0, name = "scaled\nexpression") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.2, 5), name = "% expressing") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2))

Each label expresses its canonical markers: hepatocytes ALB, ASGR1, CYP2E1, HNF4A; endothelial cells the sinusoidal program STAB2, CLEC4G, LYVE1; stellate cells DCN, COL3A1, PDGFRB; macrophages the Kupffer set MARCO, VSIG4, CD5L; and the lymphoid labels their respective CD3, KLRD1/GNLY and MS4A1/CD79A markers.

Two labels warrant an explicit note. Monocytes score highest for PECAM1, which initially looks like endothelial contamination. It is not: PECAM1 is CD31, genuinely expressed on monocytes, and the population carries monocyte-restricted FCN1 and CSF1R while lacking the endothelial-restricted VWF and EGFL7. Dendritic cells likewise carry FLT3, IRF8 and CD1C. Both labels are sound. They are nonetheless the two smallest populations (427 and 925 nuclei), which limits them later on power grounds rather than on annotation quality.

Other_T and Stellate_cell_misc are heterogeneous residual labels. They are retained so that proportions sum over the whole tissue, but no biological conclusion is drawn from their expression results.

The detailed labels

The deposit also ships a finer annotation, which subdivides only two lineages: hepatocytes by zonation and stellate cells by state. The same marker panel is applied to it.

Code 
mk_fine <- cached("markers_detailed.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  keep <- !meta[[COL_CT_FINE]] %in% DROP_LABELS
  ctf  <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])[keep])
  sub  <- mat[, which(keep)]
  normed <- log1p(multiply_cols(sub, 1e4 / colSums(sub)))
  genes  <- intersect(unique(unlist(LIVER_MARKERS)), rownames(mat))
  avg <- pseudobulk_matrix(normed[genes, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean")
  nz  <- pseudobulk_matrix(sub[genes, ],    cell_groups = ctf, method = "nonzeros")
  pct <- sweep(nz, 2, as.integer(table(ctf)), "/") * 100
  data.frame(gene = rep(rownames(avg), ncol(avg)),
             cell_type = rep(colnames(avg), each = nrow(avg)),
             avg_exp = as.vector(avg), pct_exp = as.vector(pct))
})

mk_fine <- mk_fine |> group_by(gene) |>
  mutate(z = as.numeric(scale(avg_exp))) |> ungroup()
mk_fine$gene <- factor(mk_fine$gene, levels = intersect(unlist(LIVER_MARKERS), mk_fine$gene))
mk_fine$cell_type <- factor(mk_fine$cell_type, levels = rev(sort(unique(mk_fine$cell_type))))

ggplot(mk_fine, aes(gene, cell_type)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pct_exp, colour = z)) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "#3B4CC0", mid = "grey92", high = "#B40426",
                         midpoint = 0, name = "scaled\nexpression") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(0.2, 5), name = "% expressing") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2))

The three hepatocyte zones share the hepatocyte marker profile, as they should: zonation is a gradient within a lineage, not a change of identity. The stellate substates mostly share the stellate profile.

One does not, and it matters for how the stellate results are read.

Code 
sub_expr <- cached("stellate_subtype_expr.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  sel  <- grepl("^Stellate", meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  ctf  <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])[sel])
  sb   <- mat[, which(sel)]
  nm   <- log1p(multiply_cols(sb, 1e4 / colSums(sb)))
  g <- c("DCN", "RBP1", "LRAT", "CYGB", "HGF", "COL1A1", "COL1A2",
         "PDGFRB", "TAGLN", "ACTA2", "PPARG",
         "MYH11", "MYLK", "MYL9", "NOTCH3", "RGS5")
  g <- g[g %in% rownames(mat)]
  t(pseudobulk_matrix(nm[g, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean"))
})
rownames(sub_expr) <- sub("Stellate_cell_", "", rownames(sub_expr))

kable(round(sub_expr[, c("LRAT", "DCN", "RBP1", "ACTA2", "TAGLN",
                         "MYH11", "NOTCH3", "RGS5")], 2),
      caption = "Stellate subclusters. Left: hepatic stellate identity. Right: smooth-muscle and pericyte genes.")
Stellate subclusters. Left: hepatic stellate identity. Right: smooth-muscle and pericyte genes.
LRAT DCN RBP1 ACTA2 TAGLN MYH11 NOTCH3 RGS5
activated 0.09 2.04 0.26 0.45 0.21 0.04 0.04 0.02
inactivated 0.04 0.41 0.16 1.34 0.72 1.25 0.70 0.69
misc 0.13 1.72 0.37 0.37 0.20 0.09 0.04 0.11
quiescent 0.43 2.04 0.91 0.35 0.11 0.04 0.00 0.41

The subcluster labeled Stellate_cell_inactivated carries 14-fold more MYH11 than any other stellate subcluster, plus the only appreciable NOTCH3, while holding the lowest LRAT and DCN of the four. MYH11 is smooth-muscle myosin heavy chain and is not expressed by hepatic stellate cells in any activation state, and a genuinely inactivated stellate cell that has reverted after activation retains its lipid-storing identity markers. This population has neither.

It is therefore better described as vascular smooth muscle or pericyte than as a stellate cell of any state, and it is treated that way in the detailed differential expression below, where it is relabeled Mural_VSMC. The consequences of the mislabel for the aggregate stellate results are worked through in the supplementary material.

Testing for myofibroblasts

No myofibroblast population is recovered, which bounds every fibrosis claim. TREM2 is effectively undetected here despite being present in the object, and the fibrillar collagens do not move significantly in stellate cells. It would be easy to attribute both to single-nucleus chemistry. For TREM2 that is reasonable. For the collagens it is not, and the distinction matters enough to test rather than assume.

Code 
detect <- cached("snrna_detection.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mt   <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  sel  <- meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] == "Stellate_cell"
  sb   <- mt[, which(sel)]
  one  <- rep("all", ncol(sb))
  nz   <- as.vector(pseudobulk_matrix(sb, cell_groups = one, method = "nonzeros"))
  su   <- as.vector(pseudobulk_matrix(sb, cell_groups = one, method = "sum"))
  tot  <- colSums(sb)
  list(tab = data.frame(gene = rownames(sb), pct = nz / ncol(sb) * 100,
                        cpm = su / sum(su) * 1e6),
       n_cells = ncol(sb), median_umi = median(tot))
})

col_dist <- col1a1_counts()

d <- detect$tab; d$rank <- rank(-d$cpm)
g <- c("COL3A1", "COL1A2", "COL1A1", "COL4A1", "FN1")
i <- match(g, d$gene)

# Detection expected from sequencing depth alone, if counts were Poisson.
expected <- (1 - exp(-d$cpm[i] * detect$median_umi / 1e6)) * 100

kable(data.frame(
  Gene = g,
  CPM = round(d$cpm[i]),
  `Rank of 24,615` = round(d$rank[i]),
  `% nuclei detected` = round(d$pct[i], 1),
  `% expected from depth` = round(expected, 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Observed detection in stellate nuclei against what sequencing depth alone predicts.")

Gene CPM Rank of 24,615 % nuclei detected % expected from depth
COL3A1 658 135 63.2 74.1

Observed detection tracks the depth expectation closely for every collagen tested, so there is no evidence of selective loss of this transcript class. COL3A1 is the 135th most abundant gene in stellate nuclei and is detected in 63.2% of them. Collagen transcripts are clearly capturable in this preparation.

The problem is that the cells that should express COL1A1 highly are not present!

Code 
kable(data.frame(
  `COL1A1 counts per nucleus` = c("0", "1-2", "3-4", "5-9", "10 or more"),
  `Nuclei` = c(sum(col_dist == 0), sum(col_dist %in% 1:2), sum(col_dist %in% 3:4),
               sum(col_dist %in% 5:9), sum(col_dist >= 10)),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "COL1A1 across all nuclei in the dataset.")
COL1A1 across all nuclei in the dataset.
COL1A1 counts per nucleus Nuclei
0 246390
1-2 2624
3-4 177
5-9 36
10 or more 6

The highest COL1A1 count in any nucleus in the entire dataset is 25, and only 6 nuclei carry ten or more. In a collagen-producing myofibroblast, COL1A1 is among the most abundant transcripts in the library by a wide margin. A dataset-wide maximum of 25 counts is not a detection failure, it is the absence of the cell type.

Two things most plausibly explain that absence, and neither is assay chemistry. Myofibroblasts in fibrotic tissue are embedded in dense cross-linked matrix and are recovered poorly by dissociation, a bias that is worse the less tissue there is to work with and these are from needle core biopsy samples. And the cohort tops out at F3-F4 fibrosis in ten donors, which is not end-stage disease. Consistent with both, the stellate compartment is only 4.3% of the nuclei analyzed, and stellate nuclei are among the most shallowly sequenced in the dataset at a median of 2,054 UMIs.

The consequence for reading this report is specific. Abundance and pathway-level results do not depend on recovering myofibroblasts. Statements about stellate cells describe the hepatic stellate populations that were recovered, which are largely quiescent and activated states rather than matrix-producing myofibroblasts. Nothing here should be taken as evidence about myofibroblast biology in MASH, in either direction, and the flat collagen result in particular is not evidence against fibrogenesis. A dataset built on larger tissue pieces, precision-cut slices (as I’ve done in the past) or resections rather than cores, would be the appropriate design for that question.

Axis 1: which cell types change in abundance

Composition across the disease spectrum

Code

The first panel aggregates within stage (and mirrors Figure 1b of Hong et al.), averaging the per-donor proportions so that each donor counts once regardless of how many nuclei it contributed. The second shows every donor separately. Differential abundance testing

propeller operates on per-donor proportions: logit-transformed, then moderated t-tests with empirical Bayes shrinkage across cell types. The donor is the unit throughout, so 48 donors give 48 observations, not 249,233.

Code

  group    = sub_md$condition))

8 of 12 cell types change significantly in abundance. The pattern is a single coherent event: hepatocytes are lost (0.38-fold, FDR 1.3e-06) and every significant immune population expands, led by CD4 T cells (4.6-fold) and CD8 T cells (3.4-fold).

Because proportions are compositional, these are not independent measurements. A large loss of hepatocytes mechanically raises every other fraction. The immune expansion should therefore be read as relative enrichment, not as proof of absolute immune infiltration, and that caveat applies to any proportion-based analysis of this kind.

Abundance across individual disease stages

The two-group contrast pools early and advanced MASH. Testing the stages against each other separately shows where along the progression each shift occurs.

Code 
stagewise <- cached("propeller_stagewise.rds", {
  out <- list()
  for (cc in STAGE_CONTRASTS) {
    sel <- md[[COL_STAGE]] %in% cc
    out[[paste(cc, collapse = " vs ")]] <- propeller(
      clusters = md[[COL_CT_BROAD]][sel],
      sample   = md[[COL_DONOR]][sel],
      group    = factor(as.character(md[[COL_STAGE]])[sel], levels = cc))
  }
  out
})

stage_table <- function(key) {
  r <- stagewise[[key]]
  cts <- as.character(r$BaselineProp.clusters)
  # propeller reports the ratio of the first group to the second; invert so the
  # column reads as change in the later stage relative to the earlier one.
  fc <- round(1 / r$PropRatio, 2)
  d <- data.frame(`Cell type` = ifelse(r$FDR < FDR_CUTOFF, paste0("**", cts, "**"), cts),
                  `Fold change` = fc, FDR = signif(r$FDR, 3), check.names = FALSE)
  d <- d[order(-d$`Fold change`), ]
  kable(d, row.names = FALSE,
        caption = paste0(key, ". Fold change is the later stage relative to the earlier. ",
                         "Bold: FDR < ", FDR_CUTOFF, " (", sum(r$FDR < FDR_CUTOFF),
                         " of ", nrow(r), ")."))
}

Stage-resolved abundance: where the two-group test misleads

Stellate cells are the central fibrosis cell type, yet they are flat in the two-group contrast (FDR 0.36). Splitting MASH back into its two stages explains why.

Axis 2: how each cell type is transcriptionally perturbed

Building donor-level pseudobulk

Counts are summed within each (cell type, donor) pair. This is the step that makes the donor the replication unit: one pseudo-sample per donor per cell type, carrying that donor’s condition label exactly once.

Code 
MIN_CELLS  <- 20   # a pseudo-sample must aggregate at least this many nuclei
MIN_DONORS <- 10   # a cell type needs this many donors in each group to be tested

pb <- cached("pseudobulk_broad.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  keep <- !meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS
  grp  <- paste(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]])[keep],
                as.character(meta[[COL_DONOR]])[keep], sep = "__")
  pseudobulk_matrix(mat[, which(keep)], cell_groups = grp, method = "sum")
})

  key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(colnames(pb), "__", fixed = TRUE))
  m <- data.frame(pseudosample = colnames(pb), cell_type = key[, 1],
                  donor = key[, 2], stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  m$n_cells <- as.integer(table(paste(md[[COL_CT_BROAD]], md[[COL_DONOR]],
                                      sep = "__"))[m$pseudosample])
  m$stage     <- donors$stage[match(m$donor, donors$donor)]
  m$condition <- donors$condition[match(m$donor, donors$donor)]
  m
})

Differential expression

DESeq2 per cell type, design ~ condition.

A gene is called differentially expressed on two criteria together: Benjamini-Hochberg FDR below 0.05, and an absolute log2 fold change of at least 0.25. Significance alone is a statement about confidence, not about size, and with 23 and 19 donors it admits changes too small to be interesting. The effect-size floor is applied as a filter on the results rather than as a null hypothesis in the model, so the reported p-values remain tests against no change. Enrichment analyses later in the report are unaffected as they rank all genes by the test statistic and never threshold.

Donor is deliberately absent from the design. Each donor contributes exactly one condition, so donor is nested within condition; including it would absorb the between-donor variance that constitutes the effect being tested. There is no batch variable in the deposit, so nothing else is available to adjust for.

This differs from the source paper, which ran differential expression cell-level with Seurat FindMarkers. That approach treats each nucleus as an independent replicate. With thousands of nuclei per donor the effective sample size is inflated by orders of magnitude, p-values shrink accordingly, and the resulting gene lists reflect the number of cells sequenced as much as the biology. Aggregating to the donor first is the standard correction.

Code 
de <- cached("de_primary.rds", {
  library(DESeq2)
  out <- list()
  for (ct in sort(unique(pbmeta$cell_type))) {
    sel <- pbmeta$cell_type == ct & pbmeta$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS &
           !is.na(pbmeta$condition)
    m <- pbmeta[sel, ]
    if (any(table(m$condition) < MIN_DONORS)) next
    cts <- round(pb[, m$pseudosample, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, m, ~ condition), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "MASH", "Control")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r$cell_type <- ct
    out[[ct]] <- r[order(r$padj), ]
  }
  out
})

de_severe <- cached("de_aMASH.rds", {
  library(DESeq2)
  out <- list()
  for (ct in sort(unique(pbmeta$cell_type))) {
    sel <- pbmeta$cell_type == ct & pbmeta$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS &
           pbmeta$stage %in% c("No-MASLD", "aMASH")
    m <- pbmeta[sel, ]
    m$grp <- factor(as.character(m$stage), levels = c("No-MASLD", "aMASH"))
    if (any(table(m$grp) < MIN_DONORS)) next
    cts <- round(pb[, m$pseudosample, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, m, ~ grp), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("grp", "aMASH", "No-MASLD")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r$cell_type <- ct
    out[[ct]] <- r[order(r$padj), ]
  }
  out
})

Hepatocytes are by a wide margin the most transcriptionally perturbed cell type (5,370 genes at FDR < 0.05 and |log2FC| >= 0.25), consistent with the source paper’s observation that hepatocytes carry the most change with disease severity and that MASLD heritability is enriched in them.

Differential expression at detailed resolution

The detailed annotation subdivides hepatocytes by zonation and stellate cells by state. The mural population identified above is relabeled here, since calling it an inactivated stellate cell would misattribute anything it contributes.

Code 
de_fine <- cached("de_detailed.rds", {
  library(BPCells); library(DESeq2)
  mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  meta$ct <- as.character(meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  meta$ct[meta$ct == "Stellate_cell_inactivated"] <- "Mural_VSMC"
  k <- !meta$ct %in% DROP_LABELS
  grp <- paste(meta$ct[k], meta[[COL_DONOR]][k], sep = "__")
  p <- pseudobulk_matrix(mt[, which(k)], cell_groups = grp, method = "sum")
  nc <- table(grp); key <- do.call(rbind, strsplit(colnames(p), "__", fixed = TRUE))
  dm <- unique(meta[, c(COL_DONOR, COL_STAGE)]); names(dm) <- c("donor", "stage")
  m <- data.frame(pseudosample = colnames(p), cell_type = key[, 1], donor = key[, 2],
                  n_cells = as.integer(nc[colnames(p)]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  m <- merge(m, dm, by = "donor"); m <- m[match(colnames(p), m$pseudosample), ]
  m$condition <- factor(unname(CONDITION_MAP[as.character(m$stage)]), levels = CONDITION_LEVELS)
  out <- list()
  for (ct in sort(unique(m$cell_type))) {
    sel <- m$cell_type == ct & m$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(m$condition)
    mm <- m[sel, ]; if (any(table(mm$condition) < MIN_DONORS)) next
    cts <- round(p[, mm$pseudosample, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    rownames(mm) <- mm$pseudosample
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, mm, ~ condition), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "MASH", "Control")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); out[[ct]] <- r[order(r$padj), ]
  }
  out
})

14 of the 17 detailed labels clear the donor threshold, against 10 of 12 at broad resolution. Monocytes and dendritic cells fail as before. The mural population fails too, for a reason worth noting: it contracts so sharply in disease that too few MASH donors retain enough of it to test. The correction made above therefore costs nothing.

The two axes are not the same measurement

Code 
ax <- data.frame(
  cell_type = deg$`Cell type`,
  degs      = deg$Total,
  fc        = prop_tab$`Fold change`[match(deg$`Cell type`, prop_tab$`Cell type`)],
  fdr       = prop_tab$FDR[match(deg$`Cell type`, prop_tab$`Cell type`)])
ax$abund_sig <- ifelse(ax$fdr < 0.05, "abundance FDR < 0.05", "abundance n.s.")

ggplot(ax, aes(log2(fc), degs)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = abund_sig), size = 3) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = cell_type), size = 3.1, seed = 1,
                           max.overlaps = 20, min.segment.length = 0) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("abundance FDR < 0.05" = "#C44E52",
                                 "abundance n.s." = "grey55"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "abundance change, log2(MASH / Control)",
       y = paste0("genes (", DE_RULE, ")")) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "top")

The two axes separate cleanly, and the separation is the substantive result.

Endothelial cells are the clearest case. Their abundance does not move at all (fold change 0.94, FDR 0.74), yet they carry 1,970 differentially expressed genes, the second-largest program in the dataset. A composition-only analysis would have called them unperturbed.

The reverse also holds. CD4 and CD8 T cells show the largest abundance changes in the dataset but comparatively modest expression programs (64 and 123 genes). They arrive in greater numbers without substantially altering the program they run.

Hepatocytes are the only cell type strongly perturbed on both axes: they are lost, and those that remain are extensively rewired.

Synthesis across axes: which cell types are most perturbed, and how

Code 
top_genes <- function(ct, up = TRUE, n = 4) {
  if (!ct %in% names(de)) return("not tested")
  r <- de[[ct]]
  r <- r[is_de(r), ]
  r <- r[if (up) order(-r$log2FoldChange) else order(r$log2FoldChange), ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return("-")
  paste(head(r$gene, n), collapse = ", ")
}

syn <- data.frame(
  `Cell type` = prop_tab$`Cell type`,
  `Abundance FC` = prop_tab$`Fold change`,
  `Abundance FDR` = prop_tab$FDR,
  check.names = FALSE)
syn$DEGs <- deg$Total[match(syn$`Cell type`, deg$`Cell type`)]
syn$`Top up`   <- vapply(as.character(syn$`Cell type`), top_genes, "", up = TRUE)
syn$`Top down` <- vapply(as.character(syn$`Cell type`), top_genes, "", up = FALSE)

# Rank on both axes jointly: significant abundance change and size of the
# expression program both count toward "most perturbed".
syn$abund_rank <- rank(-abs(log2(syn$`Abundance FC`)) * (syn$`Abundance FDR` < 0.05))
syn$de_rank    <- rank(-ifelse(is.na(syn$DEGs), 0, syn$DEGs))
syn <- syn[order((syn$abund_rank + syn$de_rank) / 2), ]
syn$`Abundance FDR` <- signif(syn$`Abundance FDR`, 2)
syn$DEGs <- ifelse(is.na(syn$DEGs), "not tested", format(syn$DEGs, big.mark = ","))

kable(syn[, c("Cell type", "Abundance FC", "Abundance FDR", "DEGs",
              "Top up", "Top down")], row.names = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("Cell types ranked by combined perturbation across both axes. ",
                       "Abundance FC is MASH relative to Control; DEGs are genes at ", DE_RULE, "."))

Reading the table against the question asked:

Hepatocytes are the most perturbed cell type in MASH, on both axes at once. They fall from 50.2% to 19.1% of nuclei, and the survivors carry 5,370 differentially expressed genes, more than twice any other cell type. No other population is strongly perturbed in both senses.

Endothelial cells are the most perturbed cell type that a composition analysis would miss entirely. Their abundance is unchanged, and they carry the second-largest expression program in the dataset. This is the clearest argument for separating the two axes rather than reporting “perturbation” as one quantity.

T cells are the largest abundance change and a comparatively small expression change. CD4 and CD8 T cells expand 4.6-fold and 3.4-fold, with modest programs. This is the observed evidence that they were recruited, not reprogrammed.

Macrophages change identity rather than number. A 1.4-fold abundance increase accompanies a wholesale switch from the homeostatic Kupffer program to the scar-associated program, which is the most mechanistically specific finding in the dataset.

Stellate cells are the one case where the headline contrast is misleading. They are flat in abundance between Control and MASH and carry 1,138 differentially expressed genes. Both numbers understate the situation: their expansion is confined to advanced fibrosis, and their expression program is partly a mixture artifact of a label that contains vascular mural cells.

What the expression changes mean

The DE results were checked against programs MASH is known to engage. These are recovered from the data and where the data disagree with expectation that is reported rather than smoothed over.

Code 
prog_target <- c(HSC_activation = "Stellate_cell", Scar_macrophage = "Macrophage",
                 Kupffer_homeostatic = "Macrophage", LSEC_identity = "Endothelial_cell",
                 Ductular_reaction = "Cholangiocyte")

prog <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(prog_target), function(pn) {
  r <- de[[prog_target[pn]]]
  g <- MASH_PROGRAMS[[pn]]
  s <- r[match(g, r$gene), c("gene", "log2FoldChange", "padj")]
  data.frame(program = pn, `Cell type` = unname(prog_target[pn]),
             Gene = g, log2FC = round(s$log2FoldChange, 2),
             FDR = signif(s$padj, 2), check.names = FALSE)
}))
kable(prog, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Expected MASH programs, log2 fold change MASH vs Control. NA = gene did not pass the detection filter in that cell type.")

The macrophage switch is recovered exactly as expected. Scar-associated markers rise (SPP1, GPNMB, CD9) while the homeostatic Kupffer program falls (MARCO, VSIG4, CD5L, all FDR < 0.05). This is the documented replacement of resident Kupffer cells by lipid- and scar-associated macrophages, and it appears here without being sought.

TREM2, the canonical marker for that population, is absent from the table because it failed the detection filter: it is non-zero in only 5 of 42 macrophage pseudo-samples. TREM2 is present in the object, so this is not a biological absence. Two things might be contributing: single-nucleus capture is insensitive to it, and the deposited object was built after removing genes expressed in fewer than 0.25% of cells in each donor, so lowly detected transcripts were thinned before the object was assembled.

Stellate cells appear to contradict expectation, and the contradiction is informative. ACTA2 and TAGLN both fall significantly, the opposite of the classical activation signature. Resolving this requires separating markers that are specific to hepatic stellate cells from those shared with vascular mural cells.

Code 
hsc <- c("LRAT", "DCN", "COL1A1", "COL1A2", "COL3A1")
mural <- c("MYH11", "MYL9", "TAGLN", "ACTA2", "RGS5", "NOTCH3")
r <- de$Stellate_cell
s <- r[match(c(hsc, mural), r$gene), c("gene", "log2FoldChange", "padj")]
kable(data.frame(
  Identity = c(rep("HSC-specific", length(hsc)), rep("mural / smooth muscle", length(mural))),
  Gene = c(hsc, mural), log2FC = round(s$log2FoldChange, 2),
  FDR = signif(s$padj, 2), check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Stellate compartment, split by marker identity (MASH vs Control).")
Stellate compartment, split by marker identity (MASH vs Control).
Identity Gene log2FC FDR

HSC-specific COL1A1 0.31 0.36000
HSC-specific COL1A2 0.25 0.43000
HSC-specific COL3A1 0.31 0.06000
mural / smooth muscle MYH11 -1.38 0.04000

mural / smooth muscle NOTCH3 -0.68 0.45000

The split is systematic. HSC-restricted genes rise (LRAT, the retinoid-storage enzyme that defines hepatic stellate cells, and DCN), while smooth-muscle genes fall (MYH11, MYL9, TAGLN). ACTA2 is ambiguous: it marks both activated stellate cells and vascular smooth muscle, so it cannot arbitrate. MYH11 and MYL9 can, and they are unambiguously mural.

The Stellate_cell label therefore contains a mixture of true hepatic stellate cells and vascular mural cells, and MASH shifts the mixture toward the former. The apparent loss of an activation signature is a composition shift inside the label, not deactivation of stellate cells. This is a caution about pseudobulk in general: aggregating over a heterogeneous label can invert the direction of a program.

LSEC identity is only partly perturbed. LYVE1 falls significantly, but CLEC4G and STAB2 do not, so the classical capillarization signature is not cleanly reproduced at this resolution despite endothelial cells carrying the second-largest expression program in the dataset. The endothelial perturbation is real and large but it is not well summarized by these four genes.

The ductular reaction is not detected. KRT19, KRT7, SOX9 and EPCAM all trend downward in cholangiocytes and none reach significance. Cholangiocyte abundance does rise at advanced fibrosis (3% to 3.4%), so any ductular expansion here is compositional rather than a within-cell-type program, and it is measured on the fewest donors of any tested cell type.

Benchmarking against the reference fibrosis atlas

Ramachandran et al. (2019) resolved the fibrotic niche of human cirrhotic liver and described three populations that have since become the reference framework: TREM2+CD9+ scar-associated macrophages, PLVAP+/ACKR1+ scar-associated endothelial cells, and PDGFRA+ scar-associated mesenchymal cells. All three are testable here.

The design differences matter for interpreting the result. That study profiled end-stage cirrhotic explants by single-cell RNA-seq of dissociated whole cells. This is needle-core biopsy tissue spanning F0 to F4, with ten donors at F3-F4, by single-nucleus RNA-seq.

Code 
niche <- list(
  `Scar-associated macrophage` = list(ct = "Macrophage",
    genes = c("TREM2","CD9","GPNMB","SPP1","FABP5","ACP5","LGALS3","CTSD")),
  `Resident Kupffer identity`  = list(ct = "Macrophage",
    genes = c("MARCO","VSIG4","CD5L","TIMD4","LYVE1","CETP")),
  `Scar-associated endothelium` = list(ct = "Endothelial_cell",
    genes = c("PLVAP","ACKR1","CD34","VWA1")),
  `LSEC identity`              = list(ct = "Endothelial_cell",
    genes = c("CLEC4G","CLEC4M","STAB2","OIT3","FCN2","LYVE1")),
  `PDGFRA+ mesenchyme`         = list(ct = "Stellate_cell",
    genes = c("PDGFRA","OSMR","COL1A1","COL3A1","LOXL1")))

ram <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(niche), function(nm) {
  x <- niche[[nm]]; r <- de[[x$ct]]; i <- match(x$genes, r$gene)
  data.frame(program = nm, `Cell type` = x$ct, Gene = x$genes,
             log2FC = round(r$log2FoldChange[i], 2),
             FDR = signif(r$padj[i], 2), check.names = FALSE)
}))
ram$Result <- ifelse(is.na(ram$FDR), "not detected",
              ifelse(ram$FDR >= FDR_CUTOFF | abs(ram$log2FC) < LFC_CUTOFF, "n.s.",
              ifelse(ram$log2FC > 0, "up", "down")))
kable(ram, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("Ramachandran et al. fibrotic-niche programs, tested in this ",
                       "dataset (MASH vs Control). Result applies ", DE_RULE, "."))

The scar-associated macrophage population replicates cleanly. SPP1, FABP5, ACP5, GPNMB, LGALS3 and CTSD all rise significantly, with CD9 just short of threshold and TREM2 undetectable for the reasons given in the limitations. The reciprocal half is equally clear: the resident Kupffer program falls across every marker tested.

TIMD4 is the informative one. It marks embryonically derived, self-renewing Kupffer cells, and its loss (-1.56, FDR 9.2e-06) alongside gain of the TREM2/CD9 program is the signature of resident macrophages being replaced by monocyte-derived cells. That is the mechanism Ramachandran described in cirrhosis, recovered here in a different disease, tissue source and assay.

The scar-associated endothelial population is not reproduced, and the data point the other way. PLVAP falls rather than rises. Because pseudobulk over all endothelial cells could dilute a rare subpopulation, the fraction of endothelial nuclei expressing it was tested directly at donor level.

Code 
plvap <- cached("plvap_fraction.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  sel <- meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] == "Endothelial_cell"
  v <- as.vector(as.matrix(mt["PLVAP", which(sel)]))
  data.frame(donor = meta[[COL_DONOR]][sel], stage = meta[[COL_STAGE]][sel],
             pos = v > 0)
})

pf <- aggregate(pos ~ donor, plvap, function(x) mean(x) * 100)
pf$condition <- donors$condition[match(pf$donor, donors$donor)]
tt <- t.test(pos ~ condition, data = subset(pf, !is.na(condition)))

kable(data.frame(
  Group = c("Control", "MASH"),
  `PLVAP+ endothelial nuclei (%)` = round(unname(tt$estimate), 2),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0("Donor-level fraction of PLVAP-expressing endothelial nuclei (p = ",
                   signif(tt$p.value, 2), ")."))
Donor-level fraction of PLVAP-expressing endothelial nuclei (p = 0.018).
Group PLVAP+ endothelial nuclei (%)
Control 2.73
MASH 1.68

PLVAP-positive endothelial cells are uncommon in this tissue and become significantly less common in disease, falling from 2.7% to 1.7% of endothelial nuclei (p 0.018). ACKR1 is present in the object but too sparsely detected to test.

There is also no capillarization. Sinusoidal identity is preserved across the whole progression: STAB2, CLEC4G, CLEC4M, OIT3 and FCN2 are unchanged or slightly up, and only LYVE1 declines. That is consistent with the endothelial co-expression module reported below, endo-M8, which carries STAB2, OIT3 and CLEC4M and moves upward. Endothelial cells in this cohort are transcriptionally very active, as the 1,970 differentially expressed genes show, but the direction of that activity is inflammatory rather than a loss of sinusoidal identity.

The PDGFRA+ mesenchymal population is not reproduced either. PDGFRA and the collagens do not move significantly. This is the same gap as the absent myofibroblast compartment documented in the limitations, seen from another angle. The one suggestion of the program is OSMR, which is not significant in the primary contrast but is in the advanced-fibrosis contrast.

Code 
osmr <- de_severe$Stellate_cell[de_severe$Stellate_cell$gene == "OSMR",
                                c("log2FoldChange", "padj")]
kable(data.frame(Gene = "OSMR", `Cell type` = "Stellate_cell",
                 Contrast = "control vs aMASH",
                 log2FC = round(osmr$log2FoldChange, 2),
                 FDR = signif(osmr$padj, 2), check.names = FALSE),
      row.names = FALSE)

What the pattern of hits and misses says

The two failures are not independent. Both scar-associated endothelium and PDGFRA+ mesenchyme are components of a fibrotic niche organized around myofibroblasts and scar matrix, and both are physically embedded in it. The population that does replicate, scar-associated macrophages, is the one that is not. Combined with the absent myofibroblast compartment, I think the explanation is that this tissue preparation does not recover cells resident in dense scar, rather than that the niche is absent from MASH.

Disease stage points the same way. The reference study profiled end-stage cirrhosis while the most advanced donors here are F3-F4 and there are ten of them.

This makes a concrete prediction, which is the useful form for a negative result: a MASH dataset built from precision-cut slices, resections or explants should recover the scar-associated endothelial and mesenchymal populations, while a needle-core study of comparable stage should not. What can be said from this cohort is that the macrophage arm of the fibrotic niche is present and measurable in MASH well before cirrhosis.

Pathway-level interpretation

The method I employed is GSEA (fgsea) on the MSigDB Hallmark collection, ranking genes by the DESeq2 Wald statistic. GSEA rather than over-representation testing because the pseudobulk DE produces a signed statistic for every tested gene, and ranking on all of it uses information that a hard FDR < 0.05 cutoff would discard. Hallmark rather than a finer collection because the question is what is happening to each cell type, and Hallmark’s 50 sets are curated to minimize the redundancy that makes larger collections unreadable.

Code 
gsea <- cached("gsea_primary.rds", {
  library(fgsea); library(msigdbr)
  hall <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
  sets <- split(hall$gene_symbol, hall$gs_name)
  names(sets) <- sub("^HALLMARK_", "", names(sets))
  out <- list()
  for (ct in names(de)) {
    r <- de[[ct]]; r <- r[!is.na(r$stat), ]
    stats <- setNames(r$stat, r$gene); stats <- stats[!duplicated(names(stats))]
    set.seed(42)
    res <- fgsea(sets, stats, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500, nPermSimple = 10000)
    res$cell_type <- ct
    out[[ct]] <- res[order(res$padj), ]
  }
  out
})

gs_all <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(gsea), function(ct) {
  d <- as.data.frame(gsea[[ct]]); d[, c("pathway", "NES", "padj", "cell_type")]
}))

What each cell type is doing

Code 
# Restrict to pathways that are significant somewhere with a substantial effect.
# Every significant set would be 44 rows, which is unreadable at display size;
# this keeps the strongest 25 and the panel legible.
keep_p <- unique(subset(gs_all, padj < 0.05 & abs(NES) > 1.75)$pathway)
hm <- subset(gs_all, pathway %in% keep_p)
hm$label <- ifelse(hm$padj < 0.05, "*", "")
hm$NES_show <- ifelse(hm$padj < 0.05, hm$NES, NA)

ord <- tapply(hm$NES_show, hm$pathway, function(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))
hm$pathway <- factor(hm$pathway, levels = names(sort(ord)))

ggplot(hm, aes(cell_type, pathway, fill = NES_show)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "grey92", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 3, vjust = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#3B4CC0", mid = "white", high = "#B40426",
                       midpoint = 0, na.value = "grey96", name = "NES") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       caption = "* FDR < 0.05. Grey = not significant in that cell type.") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9),
        panel.grid = element_blank())

Hepatocytes lose their specialized metabolic identity and mount an injury response. Bile acid metabolism, xenobiotic metabolism and fatty acid metabolism all fall, while the p53 pathway rises (NES 2.11, FDR 1.3e-07) alongside all three proliferation sets. That combination, loss of differentiated function with simultaneous stress signalling and cell-cycle entry, is the transcriptional signature of a compartment being damaged and regenerating. It independently reproduces the source paper’s description of reduced hepatocyte metabolic function in MASH.

Macrophages turn on cholesterol handling. CHOLESTEROL_HOMEOSTASIS is the strongest positive result in that cell type (NES 1.97), with TNFA/NF-kB signalling also up. This is the pathway-level counterpart of the gene-level switch reported above: the GPNMB, SPP1 and CD9 population that replaces homeostatic Kupffer cells is a lipid-handling, inflammatory macrophage.

Endothelial cells are inflammatory, not merely present. TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB is their top result (NES 1.79). This supplies the missing interpretation for the most striking result in the abundance analysis: endothelial cells do not change in number at all, yet carry the second-largest expression program in the dataset, and that program is inflammatory activation.

Cholangiocytes activate Hedgehog signalling (NES 1.72) together with inflammatory response, while oxidative phosphorylation falls. Hedgehog is an established fibrogenic pathway in MASH and is consistent with the cholangiocyte expansion seen at advanced fibrosis, even though the classical KRT19/KRT7 ductular markers did not reach significance gene by gene.

Proliferation moves in opposite directions, which is the clearest evidence the results are biological. Hepatocytes gain E2F targets, G2M checkpoint and mitotic spindle while NK cells lose all three, and lose them strongly (E2F_TARGETS NES -3.41, FDR 1.3e-38). The lymphoid populations that expand several-fold in abundance are therefore not expanding by local proliferation. That is consistent with recruitment, and with the earlier observation that T cells change greatly in number while changing their expression program comparatively little. It is consistent with recruitment rather than a demonstration of it. That said, this dataset is a single snapshot per donor and cannot establish where those cells came from.

Resolving the signature

Is the hepatocyte response zonal?

Hepatocytes split into pericentral, periportal and interzonal, and the analysis so far appears to say the pericentral zone is most perturbed. However, that reading does not survive scrutiny as the zones differ in donor coverage and in cell numbers, so they differ in power before any biology is considered.

Code 
z <- c("Hepatocyte_pericentral", "Hepatocyte_periportal", "Hepatocyte_interzonal")
lab <- c("PC", "PP", "IZ")
cz <- Reduce(intersect, lapply(de_fine[z], function(r) r$gene))
fz <- sapply(de_fine[z], function(r) r$log2FoldChange[match(cz, r$gene)])
az <- sapply(de_fine[z], function(r) r$padj[match(cz, r$gene)])
colnames(fz) <- colnames(az) <- lab
sigz <- !is.na(az) & az < FDR_CUTOFF & abs(fz) >= LFC_CUTOFF
shared <- rowSums(sigz) == 3
concordant <- sum(abs(rowSums(sign(fz[shared, ]))) == 3, na.rm = TRUE)

# Donors contributing a testable pseudo-sample, counted the same way the DE did.
zone_donors <- sapply(z, function(x) {
  k <- md[[COL_CT_FINE]] == x
  n <- table(md[[COL_DONOR]][k])
  d <- unique(md[, c(COL_DONOR, "condition")])
  d <- d[match(names(n), d[[COL_DONOR]]), ]
  ok <- n >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(d$condition)
  paste(sum(ok & d$condition == "Control"), "/", sum(ok & d$condition == "MASH"))
})

kable(data.frame(
  Zone = lab,
  `Donors (Control / MASH)` = zone_donors,
  `Nuclei` = format(sapply(z, function(x) sum(md[[COL_CT_FINE]] == x)), big.mark = ","),
  `DEGs` = sapply(z, function(x) sum(is_de(de_fine[[x]]))),
  `Median |log2FC|` = round(apply(abs(fz), 2, median, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Hepatocyte zones: differential expression against available power.")
Hepatocyte zones: differential expression against available power.
Zone Donors (Control / MASH) Nuclei DEGs Median |log2FC|
PC 23 / 18 48,614 5070 0.294
PP 23 / 16 37,872 3707 0.291
IZ 23 / 12 11,811 2502 0.318

The DEG counts track donor and nucleus numbers, not effect size. Median absolute fold change is essentially identical across the three zones (0.29, 0.29, 0.32), and the pairwise correlation of fold changes between zones is 0.82 to 0.86.

Of the 1,824 genes significant in all three zones, 1,824 agree in direction. That is 100%.

Hepatocytes mount one disease program, not three zonal ones. This matters for how the result is used. If the response were zone-restricted, any intervention would have to reach the right zone to be effective. It is not: zonal identity is preserved as a baseline, and the MASH response is superimposed on all three compartments in the same direction and at the same magnitude.

Module-level structure

Individual genes are a difficult unit to act on. The source study built co-expression modules with hdWGCNA and deposited both the module definitions and per-cell harmonized module eigengenes. Those are reused here rather than recomputed, but tested at the donor level, which their own analysis did not do.

Code 
mod_res <- cached("module_de.rds", {
  dirp <- "data/unzipped/Zenodo/hdWGCNA_results"
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  meta$cond <- unname(CONDITION_MAP[meta[[COL_STAGE]]])
  do.call(rbind, lapply(c("hepatocyte","stellate_cell","endothelial_cell","cholangiocyte"),
    function(tag) {
      x <- read.delim(gzfile(file.path(dirp, paste0(tag, "_hME.txt.gz"))), check.names = FALSE)
      rownames(x) <- x[[1]]; x <- x[, -1, drop = FALSE]
      x <- x[, colnames(x) != "grey", drop = FALSE]
      cm <- intersect(rownames(x), rownames(meta))
      x <- x[cm, , drop = FALSE]; mm <- meta[cm, ]
      dmean <- t(sapply(colnames(x), function(k)
        tapply(x[[k]], mm[[COL_DONOR]], mean, na.rm = TRUE)))
      dn <- unique(mm[, c(COL_DONOR, "cond")]); rownames(dn) <- dn[[COL_DONOR]]
      dn <- dn[colnames(dmean), ]; kp <- !is.na(dn$cond)
      r <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rownames(dmean), function(k) {
        tt <- t.test(dmean[k, kp] ~ factor(dn$cond[kp], levels = CONDITION_LEVELS))
        data.frame(cell_type = tag, module = k,
                   diff = unname(tt$estimate[2] - tt$estimate[1]), p = tt$p.value)
      }))
      r$FDR <- p.adjust(r$p, "BH"); r
    }))
})

sig_mod <- subset(mod_res, FDR < 0.05)
sig_mod <- sig_mod[order(sig_mod$FDR), ]
kable(data.frame(
  `Cell type` = sig_mod$cell_type, Module = sig_mod$module,
  `Change in MASH` = round(sig_mod$diff, 2), FDR = signif(sig_mod$FDR, 2),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Co-expression modules differentially expressed between MASH and Control, tested on per-donor mean module eigengenes.")

16 of 37 deposited modules move significantly at donor level. The distribution matches the gene-level results closely: 6 of nine endothelial modules shift despite endothelial cells not changing in abundance at all, which is the same dissociation reported earlier arriving through an independent construction.

The largest hepatocyte effect is Hep-M12, down by 2.38 (FDR 4.9e-08). Its highest-connectivity members are FGB, FGG, FGA, FGL1, CP, CYP3A5 and PCK1: fibrinogen synthesis, copper transport, drug metabolism and gluconeogenesis. It is a hepatocyte secretory and metabolic identity program, and it is the single most-perturbed coordinated unit found anywhere in this analysis.

Two further observations: The upregulated hepatocyte module Hep-M6 contains PPARA, MLXIPL and PLIN5, and the upregulated stellate module HSC-M3 contains NR1H4. Both are nuclear receptors with existing pharmacology in metabolic liver disease, which is a reassuring sign that the signature is not disconnected from known biology. Nothing here directly tests any drug, and no directional inference about a therapeutic effect follows from a module changing.

Discussion

What this dataset can and cannot say about MASH therapeutics

MASH now has FDA approved drugs and a crowded development pipeline, and a natural question is whether a dataset like this speaks to any of them. It does, but only in a specific and limited way.

An observational cross-sectional cohort of 48 donors can establish two things about a drug target: whether the target is expressed in the cell type the drug is meant to act on, and whether the program that target controls is among the things disease has perturbed. Those are questions about whether a mechanism is engageable and relevant in human MASH liver.

With that stated, the dataset does separate the pipeline into three groups.

Code 
drug_expr <- cached("drug_target_expr.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  k <- !meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]] %in% DROP_LABELS
  ctf <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_BROAD]])[k]); sb <- mt[, which(k)]
  nmz <- log1p(multiply_cols(sb, 1e4 / colSums(sb)))
  gg <- c("THRB","DIO1","GLP1R","GCGR","GIPR","KLB","FGFR1","NR1H4","NR0B2",
          "PPARA","PPARD","PPARG","ITGAV","ITGB1","ITGB6","ITGB8",
          "TGFB1","TGFBR1","TGFBR2","LOXL2","LOX","LOXL1")
  present <- gg[gg %in% rownames(mt)]
  a <- pseudobulk_matrix(nmz[present, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean")
  n <- pseudobulk_matrix(sb[present, ],  cell_groups = ctf, method = "nonzeros")
  list(avg = a, pct = sweep(n, 2, as.integer(table(ctf)), "/") * 100,
       absent = setdiff(gg, present))
})

targ <- data.frame(
  Target = c("THRB", "GCGR", "GLP1R", "GIPR", "KLB", "NR1H4", "PPARA", "PPARD",
             "PPARG", "ITGAV", "ITGB6", "TGFB1", "LOXL2", "LOX"),
  Drug = c("resmetirom", "survodutide (glucagon arm)", "semaglutide",
           "tirzepatide (GIP arm)", "FGF21 analogues", "FXR agonists",
           "elafibranor, lanifibranor", "seladelpar, elafibranor",
           "lanifibranor", "integrin inhibitors", "integrin avb6 inhibitors",
           "TGF-beta blockade", "simtuzumab", "LOX inhibitors"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

look <- function(g, what) {
  if (g %in% drug_expr$absent) return(NA_real_)
  m <- drug_expr[[what]]
  if (!g %in% rownames(m)) return(NA_real_)
  max(m[g, ])
}
where <- function(g) {
  if (g %in% drug_expr$absent) return("not in object")
  colnames(drug_expr$avg)[which.max(drug_expr$avg[g, ])]
}
targ$`Highest in`  <- sapply(targ$Target, where)
targ$`Mean expr`   <- round(sapply(targ$Target, look, "avg"), 2)
targ$`% expressing`<- round(sapply(targ$Target, look, "pct"), 1)
kable(targ, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Where each target is expressed. Mean expression and percent are for the cell type where the target is highest.")

Targets that are well represented in this tissue

THR-beta (resmetirom). THRB is expressed in 88.6% of hepatocytes, the highest of any cell type, and it is not itself altered in disease. The programs it regulates are hepatocyte fatty acid metabolism, bile acid metabolism and xenobiotic metabolism are all significantly depleted in MASH here, and that loss of differentiated metabolic function is the dominant hepatocyte finding in this report. So the receptor is abundant and intact in exactly the cell type whose metabolic program has degraded. That is a coherent target-tissue picture, and it is the most straightforwardly supported mechanism in the dataset.

FXR (obeticholic acid and successors). NR1H4 is well expressed in both hepatocytes and stellate cells. More informative than the receptor is its output: NR0B2, the canonical FXR target gene, is strongly reduced in hepatocytes (log2FC -1.48, FDR 7.7e-10), alongside the depleted bile acid program. FXR signalling output is measurably lower in MASH hepatocytes in this cohort. Whether restoring it is beneficial is a clinical question this dataset cannot address, and the mixed clinical history of FXR agonism is a reminder that pathway restoration and patient benefit are different things.

PPAR-alpha (elafibranor, lanifibranor). PPARA is well expressed in hepatocytes and unchanged in disease, and it sits inside Hep-M6, one of the hepatocyte modules that moves significantly. PPARG is macrophage-biased, and macrophages show the strongest cholesterol-homeostasis enrichment in the dataset, which is at least consistent with a lipid-handling role for the myeloid arm of a pan-PPAR agent. PPARD is poorly detected in every cell type here, so this dataset can say little about selective delta agonism.

Glucagon (survodutide’s glucagon arm). This one differs, and the distinction is worth drawing. GCGR is expressed in 47.7% of hepatocytes and is modestly reduced in MASH (log2FC -0.36, FDR 0.0096). Unlike the GLP-1 and GIP components, the glucagon arm of a dual agonist has a direct hepatocyte target that is measurable in this tissue. That makes glucagon-containing dual agonists the incretin-class agents this dataset can actually say something about.

Targets whose liver action is not visible in this dataset

GLP-1 (semaglutide). GLP1R is not present in the object at all. This is not a detection failure peculiar to this study: hepatocytes are not generally held to express GLP-1 receptor, and the hepatic benefit of GLP-1 agonism is understood to be largely indirect, through weight loss, glycaemic control and adipose signalling. The consequence is simply that a liver transcriptomic atlas is the wrong instrument for evaluating it. Its absence here is uninformative about the drug.

GIP (tirzepatide’s GIP arm). GIPR is effectively undetected in hepatocytes. The same reasoning applies.

FGF21 analogues. The obligate co-receptor KLB is detected in only 18.2% of hepatocytes, and FGFR1 is essentially absent from hepatocytes while being present on stellate cells. FGF21 biology is substantially adipose-directed, so a liver dataset again under-reports the mechanism.

Anti-fibrotic targets: this dataset cannot evaluate them

Code 
af <- c("LOX", "LOXL1", "LOXL2", "ITGB6", "ITGB1", "ITGAV", "TGFB1", "TGFBR1", "TGFBR2")
af <- af[!af %in% drug_expr$absent]
kable(data.frame(
  Target = af,
  `Highest in` = sapply(af, where),
  `Mean expr` = round(sapply(af, look, "avg"), 2),
  `% expressing` = round(sapply(af, look, "pct"), 1),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Anti-fibrotic drug targets, at the cell type where each is highest.")
