The lysyl oxidases are the clearest case. LOX is essentially undetected, LOXL1 and LOXL2 are detected in a few percent of stellate cells, and LOXL2 does not change significantly with disease. ITGB6, the target of alpha-v-beta-6 integrin inhibition, is effectively absent. TGFB1 is low in every cell type, and the TGF-beta signalling program is not significantly enriched in stellate cells. Read naively, this would look like a dataset arguing against anti-fibrotic targets.

That reading would be wrong, and the reason is documented earlier in this report. These drugs act on collagen-producing myofibroblasts, and this dataset does not contain them: the highest COL1A1 count in any nucleus across the entire atlas is 25, and the scar-associated endothelial and mesenchymal populations from the reference cirrhosis atlas both fail to appear while the scar-associated macrophage population replicates cleanly. The most likely explanation for all of it is that needle-core biopsy tissue does not recover cells resident in dense scar matrix.

So the correct statement is not that this dataset provides weak support for anti-fibrotic mechanisms. It is that this dataset cannot assess them, because the cell population those drugs target is missing from it for reasons of tissue sampling rather than biology. An apparent absence of a drug target is only evidence when the cells that would express it were recoverable in the first place. The one anti-fibrotic-adjacent target that does move is ITGAV in stellate cells (log2FC 0.42, FDR 0.0013), which is suggestive and no more.

Does the data support combination therapy?

Not directly, and any dataset of this design would struggle to. What it does provide is a structural argument, which is weaker but not empty.

The central result of this report is that MASH perturbation is distributed across cell types along two independent axes, and that the axes do not coincide. Hepatocytes lose a metabolic program and are depleted. Macrophages switch identity from resident Kupffer to scar-associated without much change in number. Endothelial cells carry the second-largest expression program in the dataset with no abundance change at all, and its content is inflammatory. Lymphocytes expand several-fold with comparatively little transcriptional change.

A hepatocyte-directed metabolic agent, whether a thyromimetic, an incretin or a PPAR agonist, addresses the first of those compartments. Nothing in this data suggests it would directly reach the macrophage identity switch or the endothelial inflammatory program, both of which are large, statistically robust and confined to cell types the metabolic targets are not expressed in. That distribution is a reason to expect that a single-compartment intervention leaves a substantial part of the measured disease untouched.

What this dataset cannot do is tell you which second agent to employ. Adjudicating a metabolic-plus-anti-fibrotic combination specifically would require measuring the fibrotic compartment, and this tissue preparation does not recover it (but at least we now know that). A study built on precision-cut liver slices (like the kind I’ve done in the past at Pliant), resections or explants, where myofibroblasts and the scar-resident niche are retained, is the design that could potentially answer the direct anti-fibrotic question.

Limitations

Compositional dependence. Proportions sum to one, so the loss of half the hepatocyte compartment mechanically inflates every other fraction. The immune expansions are relative enrichments. Distinguishing that from absolute infiltration would require a cell-number-per-unit-tissue measurement that dissociation-based data cannot provide.

No batch variable. The deposit carries no sequencing run, chemistry or processing-date column, so no technical covariate could be tested or adjusted for. The cohort is single-center, which limits the risk, but this cannot be verified from what was deposited.

Fibrosis is available only as a dichotomy. The source study staged fibrosis on the full Brunt/Kleiner F0-F4 scale, but used it only to define the eMASH (F0-2) and aMASH (F3-4) groups, and the per-donor stage was not deposited. The metadata carries disease group and nothing else clinical: no fibrosis stage, no activity score, no ALT, and no age, sex or BMI. The finest fibrosis comparison possible here is therefore the two-bin eMASH-versus-aMASH contrast, on 9 and 10 donors. No dose-response across F0 to F4 can be tested, and the stellate result above should be read with that in mind: it is a difference between two coarse fibrosis bins, not a gradient. The same constraint rules out relating cell-type proportions to clinical severity, which the source paper was able to do because it had the clinical table.

Label heterogeneity is a real constraint. The stellate result demonstrates that pseudobulk over a mixed label can invert a program’s apparent direction. The same risk applies in principle to every label used here. It was caught in this instance because the expected direction was known in advance and checked.

Controls are not healthy volunteers. They are biopsies from people undergoing clinical procedures with no MASLD diagnosis. A baseline of stellate activation and immune presence is expected, and comparisons are against that baseline, not against normal liver.

Unequal and modest group sizes. The stage-resolved contrasts rest on 6 to 10 donors per arm. The eMASH-versus-aMASH stellate result does not survive multiple-testing correction and is reported as suggestive for that reason.

Reused integration and inherited annotation. The analysis relies on the deposited Liger integration and cluster labels rather than re-deriving them. That is deliberate: the labels were validated against canonical markers before use, and re-clustering a published, already-integrated object risks recapitulating the original result rather than testing it. It does mean any error in the deposited annotation propagates here, as the stellate inactivated subcluster illustrates. That case also shows the check working: the mixture was detectable from marker expression, from unbiased enrichment and from the subcluster-level profile, without re-clustering anything.

Supplementary

Within-lineage resolution

Two lineages subdivide in the deposited annotation, and both subdivide along an axis MASH acts on. This is where the detailed labels earn their place.

Code 
sub_frac <- function(prefix) {
  s  <- md[grepl(prefix, md[[COL_CT_FINE]]), ]
  tb <- table(s[[COL_DONOR]], s[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  pr <- sweep(tb, 1, rowSums(tb), "/") * 100
  st <- donors$stage[match(rownames(pr), donors$donor)]
  data.frame(donor = rep(rownames(pr), ncol(pr)),
             subtype = rep(colnames(pr), each = nrow(pr)),
             pct = as.vector(pr), stage = rep(st, ncol(pr)))
}

st_frac  <- sub_frac("^Stellate")
hep_frac <- sub_frac("^Hepatocyte")

ggplot(rbind(st_frac, hep_frac), aes(stage, pct, fill = stage)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ subtype, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#4C72B0", "#DD8452", "#C44E52", "#8172B3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "% of parent lineage") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

No-MASLD MASL eMASH aMASH
Stellate_cell_activated 24.5 7.7 22.7 29.1
Stellate_cell_inactivated 14.3 4.5 2.6 5.1

Hepatocyte zonation shifts consistently: the pericentral fraction rises across the progression while periportal and interzonal fractions fall. Given that hepatocytes are simultaneously halving in absolute proportion, this is a relative change in which zonal identity survives, not evidence that pericentral hepatocytes increase in number.

The stellate substates move much less than their names suggest. The activated fraction is already 24.5% in controls and reaches only 29.1% in advanced MASH. The controls are liver biopsies from people undergoing clinical procedures rather than healthy volunteers, so a non-trivial baseline of stellate activation is plausible.

The substate that does move sharply is inactivated, which falls from 14.3% to 5.1%. That turns out to matter more than the activated fraction, and it is taken up in detail below, after the enrichment results supply a second line of evidence about what that subcluster actually contains.

How these substate labels were produced is relevant to reading them. The source paper’s supplementary methods describe subclustering all donors together, then subclustering disease and control cells separately, and assigning a substate only where both analyses agreed. Cells that disagreed were labeled Unidentified, and subclusters showing ectopic marker expression were labeled misc. That is a conservative procedure, but it means the substate assignments are not independent of disease status, so substate proportions compared across disease groups should be read as descriptive rather than as a clean test.

Is this a technical gradient?

Enrichment on pseudobulk is vulnerable to a specific failure: proliferation and biosynthesis sets are loaded with highly expressed housekeeping genes, so a systematic difference in capture depth between groups can produce a sweep of significant hits that reflect nothing biological. Three checks decide whether that is happening here.

Code 
sig <- subset(gs_all, padj < 0.05)
spread <- aggregate(NES ~ pathway, sig, function(x) c(n = length(x), lo = min(x), hi = max(x)))
spread <- data.frame(pathway = spread$pathway, n_types = spread$NES[, "n"],
                     NES_min = round(spread$NES[, "lo"], 2),
                     NES_max = round(spread$NES[, "hi"], 2))
spread <- spread[order(-spread$n_types), ][1:6, ]

pb_sel <- pbmeta$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(pbmeta$condition)
depth  <- tapply(colSums(pb[, pbmeta$pseudosample[pb_sel]]) /
                 pbmeta$n_cells[pb_sel], pbmeta$condition[pb_sel], median)

kable(spread, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Pathways significant in the most cell types, with the range of their enrichment scores.")
Pathways significant in the most cell types, with the range of their enrichment scores.
pathway n_types NES_min NES_max
MYC_TARGETS_V1 8 -2.92 1.65
TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB 8 -1.51 1.85
ALLOGRAFT_REJECTION 7 -2.06 1.76
INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE 7 -2.25 1.54
INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE 7 -2.27 1.57
MITOTIC_SPINDLE 6 -1.97 1.76

The most widely significant pathways change sign between cell types. MYC_TARGETS_V1 runs from NES -2.92 to 1.65 depending on which cell type is examined. A depth artifact would push every cell type in the same direction.

Median counts per nucleus are comparable between groups (2019 in Control, 2202 in MASH), and DESeq2 models library size explicitly in any case.

The leading-edge genes are process-specific, not housekeeping. The strongest single result in the dataset is loss of E2F_TARGETS in NK cells, and its leading edge is RRM2, MELK, BIRC5, MCM4, MCM6, ORC6, CENPE: replication and mitotic machinery, with no ribosomal protein genes at all.

The results are therefore read as biological.

Localizing the mixture to one subcluster

The annotation section established that the subcluster labeled Stellate_cell_inactivated is vascular mural rather than stellate. This section works out what that mislabel does to the aggregate stellate results, which is where it matters.

One point of context first. The source paper defines its inactivated state on PDGFRB, TAGLN, ACTA2 and PPARG, so ACTA2 and TAGLN are markers of that state rather than of activation. Loss of those genes from the stellate compartment therefore has two candidate explanations, mural contamination or genuine loss of an inactivated stellate population, and they are separable because they predict different behavior from smooth-muscle genes that appear in neither panel.

Code 
sub_expr <- cached("stellate_subtype_expr.rds", {
  library(BPCells)
  mat  <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds"))
  sel  <- grepl("^Stellate", meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])
  ctf  <- factor(as.character(meta[[COL_CT_FINE]])[sel])
  sb   <- mat[, which(sel)]
  nm   <- log1p(multiply_cols(sb, 1e4 / colSums(sb)))
  g <- c("DCN", "RBP1", "LRAT", "CYGB", "HGF", "COL1A1", "COL1A2",
         "PDGFRB", "TAGLN", "ACTA2", "PPARG",
         "MYH11", "MYLK", "MYL9", "NOTCH3", "RGS5")
  g <- g[g %in% rownames(mat)]
  t(pseudobulk_matrix(nm[g, ], cell_groups = ctf, method = "mean"))
})

Mean log-normalized expression by stellate subcluster. Left block: hepatic stellate identity. Middle: the paper’s inactivated-state panel. Right: smooth-muscle and pericyte genes used by neither panel.
LRAT DCN RBP1 COL1A1 ACTA2 TAGLN PDGFRB MYH11 NOTCH3 RGS5
activated 0.09 2.04 0.26 0.64 0.45 0.21 1.10 0.04 0.04 0.02
inactivated 0.04 0.41 0.16 0.42 1.34 0.72 1.37 1.25 0.70 0.69

The inactivated subcluster carries 14-fold more MYH11 than any other stellate subcluster, along with the only appreciable NOTCH3, while showing the lowest LRAT and DCN of the four.

That combination decides the question. MYH11 is smooth-muscle myosin heavy chain and is not expressed by hepatic stellate cells in any activation state. A genuinely inactivated stellate cell, one that has reverted after activation, retains its lipid-storing identity markers; this population has the least LRAT and DCN of any subcluster while uniquely expressing MYH11 and NOTCH3. It is better described as vascular smooth muscle or pericyte than as a stellate cell of any state.

That mural population also declines across the progression, falling from 14.3% to 5.1% of the compartment, which is the right shape to inflate an apparent loss of contractile genes when the whole label is aggregated.

How much of the effect is composition?

The tempting conclusion is that the entire contractile signal is a mixture artifact. That is testable in two ways, and the test does not fully support it.

Code 
# 1. Rebuild the stellate pseudobulk with the mural subcluster removed.
# 2. Test inside single subtypes, where composition is fixed by construction and
#    any remaining change must be a within-cell-type effect.
decomp <- cached("stellate_decompose.rds", {
  library(BPCells); library(DESeq2)
  meta <- readRDS(cache_path("meta.rds")); mt <- open_matrix_dir("bpcells_counts")
  dn <- unique(meta[, c(COL_DONOR, COL_STAGE)])
  cnd <- setNames(unname(CONDITION_MAP[dn[[COL_STAGE]]]), dn[[COL_DONOR]])

  de_on <- function(subtypes) {
    sel <- meta[[COL_CT_FINE]] %in% subtypes
    grp <- paste0("g__", meta[[COL_DONOR]][sel])
    p <- pseudobulk_matrix(mt[, which(sel)], cell_groups = grp, method = "sum")
    n <- table(grp)[colnames(p)]; dono <- sub("g__", "", colnames(p))
    keep <- n >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(cnd[dono])
    cts <- round(p[, keep, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    cd <- data.frame(condition = factor(cnd[dono[keep]], levels = CONDITION_LEVELS),
                     row.names = colnames(cts))
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, cd, ~ condition), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("condition", "MASH", "Control")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r$n_control <- sum(cd$condition == "Control")
    r$n_mash <- sum(cd$condition == "MASH"); r
  }
  list(
    hsc_only  = de_on(c("Stellate_cell_quiescent", "Stellate_cell_activated",
                        "Stellate_cell_misc")),
    quiescent = de_on("Stellate_cell_quiescent"),
    activated = de_on("Stellate_cell_activated"))
})

pull <- function(r, g) {
  i <- match(g, r$gene)
  sprintf("%+.2f%s", r$log2FoldChange[i],
          ifelse(is_de(r)[i], "*", ""))
}
gg <- c("TAGLN", "ACTA2", "MYH11", "MYL9", "LRAT", "COL1A1", "COL3A1")
kable(data.frame(
  Gene = gg,
  `All stellate` = pull(de$Stellate_cell, gg),
  `Mural removed` = pull(decomp$hsc_only, gg),
  `Quiescent only` = pull(decomp$quiescent, gg),
  `Activated only` = pull(decomp$activated, gg),
  check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE,
  caption = paste0("log2 fold change, MASH vs Control, as the mural subcluster is ",
                   "removed and then as the test is confined within single subtypes. * = ", DE_RULE, "."))

ACTA2 -1.14* -0.77* -0.96* -0.50
MYH11 -1.38* -0.89 -1.01 -1.16
MYL9 -0.54* -0.40* -0.59* -0.24

The two contractile genes behave differently, and the distinction matters.

MYH11 loses significance as soon as the mural subcluster is removed and stays non-significant inside both subtypes. That is what a pure composition effect looks like, and it confirms the mural reading.

TAGLN does not. It remains strongly depleted inside the quiescent subcluster and inside the activated subcluster, tested separately, where composition is fixed by construction and cannot contribute. That is a real transcriptional change within hepatic stellate cells.

So both mechanisms are operating, and an earlier reading of this result as purely a mixture artifact would have been wrong. A mural population is inflating the aggregate signal, which is why MYOGENESIS weakens from -1.76 to non-significance once those cells are excluded. Underneath it there is a genuine, subtype-independent downregulation of TAGLN in stellate cells. What the data do not support is the simple statement that stellate cells are losing their activation program wholesale: LRAT rises rather than falls, and the fibrillar collagens do not move significantly in either direction. That last point should not be read as evidence against fibrogenesis either: as quantified in the limitations, this dataset contains no collagen-producing myofibroblast population to detect a change in.

This remains a caution about the deposited annotation, and it is only visible because the deposit ships substate labels alongside the broad ones. It is also a concrete illustration of the general hazard, with the qualification that decomposing the effect matters: pseudobulk over a mixed label can exaggerate a program, and separating composition from within-cell-type change requires testing at a level where composition cannot vary.

Comparison with the source paper’s own enrichment

The source paper ran its own enrichment on the same tissue, reported in its Supplementary Table 3. Comparing against it tests whether the pathway-level conclusions here depend on the analytical choices made in this report.

Four differences matter when reading the comparison. Their differential expression was cell-level Seurat FindMarkers, against donor-level pseudobulk here. Their enrichment was over-representation testing with enrichR on thresholded gene lists, against GSEA on the full ranking here. Their gene sets were GO Biological Process, against Hallmark here, and the two collections do not map one-to-one. And their comparison pooled MASL into the reference group as “nonMASH”, where the primary contrast here holds MASL out. Their table also reports only the top four terms in each direction, so a term missing from it is not evidence that they found nothing.

Code 
# Terms as reported in Hong et al. Supplementary Table 3 (GO Biological Process,
# enrichR, MASH vs nonMASH). Quoted here as reference values; every value in the
# "this report" columns is computed from the GSEA above.
paper <- data.frame(
  cell_type = c("Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte", "Hepatocyte",
                "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte",
                "Stellate_cell", "Stellate_cell",
                "Endothelial_cell", "Endothelial_cell"),
  paper_term = c("cholesterol biosynthetic process", "steroid metabolic process",
                 "drug catabolic process", "cellular amino acid catabolic process",
                 "mitochondrial electron transport", "Notch signaling pathway",
                 "regulation of canonical Wnt signaling",
                 "muscle contraction", "collagen fibril organization",
                 "cellular response to interferon-gamma",
                 "positive regulation of cell migration"),
  paper_dir = c("up", "down", "down", "down",
                "down", "up", "up",
                "down", "up",
                "down", "up"),
  hallmark = c("CHOLESTEROL_HOMEOSTASIS", "BILE_ACID_METABOLISM",
               "XENOBIOTIC_METABOLISM", "FATTY_ACID_METABOLISM",
               "OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION", "NOTCH_SIGNALING",
               "WNT_BETA_CATENIN_SIGNALING",
               "MYOGENESIS", "EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION",
               "INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE", "EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

lookup <- function(ct, pw, field) {
  r <- gs_all[gs_all$cell_type == ct & gs_all$pathway == pw, ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return(NA_real_)
  r[[field]][1]
}
paper$NES <- mapply(lookup, paper$cell_type, paper$hallmark, "NES")
paper$FDR <- mapply(lookup, paper$cell_type, paper$hallmark, "padj")
paper$this_dir <- ifelse(is.na(paper$NES), NA,
                  ifelse(paper$FDR >= 0.05, "n.s.",
                  ifelse(paper$NES > 0, "up", "down")))
paper$agrees <- ifelse(paper$this_dir == "n.s.", "not significant",
                ifelse(paper$this_dir == paper$paper_dir, "agrees", "opposite"))

kable(data.frame(
  `Cell type` = paper$cell_type,
  `Paper GO term` = paper$paper_term,
  `Paper` = paper$paper_dir,
  `Matched Hallmark set` = paper$hallmark,
  `NES` = round(paper$NES, 2),
  `FDR` = signif(paper$FDR, 2),
  `Verdict` = paper$agrees,

Hepatocyte metabolic reprogramming replicates completely. All four reported directions agree: cholesterol handling up, and steroid, drug-catabolic and fatty-acid metabolism down. Two methods that share nothing except the underlying tissue reach the same conclusion, which is the strongest form of corroboration available here.

Their table contains the stellate result independently. Supplementary Table 3 reports muscle contraction as significantly depleted in stellate cells in MASH. That is the same signal as the MYOGENESIS depletion above (NES -1.76), recovered from different data processing, a different differential expression method and a different gene set collection.

This matters for how the mural-cell interpretation should be read. The observation is not particular to this pipeline: it is present in the source paper’s own supplementary results, where it is reported without interpretation. What this report adds is the explanation, that the depletion reflects loss of a mural population carried inside the stellate label rather than a change in stellate contractile state.

Where the two analyses diverge

Code 
# Their reference group pools MASL with controls. Rerunning the four cell types
# their table covers under that definition separates disagreements caused by the
# grouping from disagreements caused by method.
gsea_pooled <- cached("gsea_pooled.rds", {
  library(fgsea); library(msigdbr)
  hall <- msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
  sets <- split(hall$gene_symbol, hall$gs_name)
  names(sets) <- sub("^HALLMARK_", "", names(sets))
  pm <- pbmeta
  pm$grp <- ifelse(pm$stage %in% c("No-MASLD", "MASL"), "nonMASH",
            ifelse(pm$stage %in% c("eMASH", "aMASH"), "MASH", NA))
  out <- list()
  for (ct in c("Hepatocyte", "Cholangiocyte", "Stellate_cell", "Endothelial_cell")) {
    sel <- pm$cell_type == ct & pm$n_cells >= MIN_CELLS & !is.na(pm$grp)
    m <- pm[sel, ]; m$grp <- factor(m$grp, levels = c("nonMASH", "MASH"))
    cts <- round(pb[, m$pseudosample, drop = FALSE]); mode(cts) <- "integer"
    cts <- cts[rowSums(cts > 0) >= ceiling(ncol(cts) / 3), , drop = FALSE]
    dds <- DESeq(DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(cts, m, ~ grp), quiet = TRUE)
    r <- as.data.frame(results(dds, contrast = c("grp", "MASH", "nonMASH")))
    r$gene <- rownames(r); r <- r[!is.na(r$stat), ]
    st <- setNames(r$stat, r$gene); st <- st[!duplicated(names(st))]
    set.seed(42)
    out[[ct]] <- as.data.frame(fgsea(sets, st, minSize = 10, maxSize = 500,
                                     nPermSimple = 10000))
  }
  out
})

pooled_get <- function(ct, pw) {
  r <- gsea_pooled[[ct]][gsea_pooled[[ct]]$pathway == pw, ]
  if (!nrow(r)) return(c(NA, NA))
  c(r$NES[1], r$padj[1])
}
diverge <- data.frame(
  `Cell type` = c("Stellate_cell", "Endothelial_cell", "Cholangiocyte", "Cholangiocyte"),
  `Hallmark set` = c("EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION", "INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE",
                     "NOTCH_SIGNALING", "WNT_BETA_CATENIN_SIGNALING"),
  check.names = FALSE)
mine <- t(mapply(function(ct, pw) c(lookup(ct, pw, "NES"), lookup(ct, pw, "padj")),
                 diverge$`Cell type`, diverge$`Hallmark set`))
pool <- t(mapply(pooled_get, diverge$`Cell type`, diverge$`Hallmark set`))
diverge$`NES (MASL held out)`   <- round(mine[, 1], 2)
diverge$`FDR (held out)`        <- signif(mine[, 2], 2)
diverge$`NES (MASL pooled in)`  <- round(pool[, 1], 2)
diverge$`FDR (pooled in)`       <- signif(pool[, 2], 2)
kable(diverge, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "The four disagreements, evaluated under both reference-group definitions.")
The four disagreements, evaluated under both reference-group definitions.
Cell type Hallmark set NES (MASL held out) FDR (held out) NES (MASL pooled in) FDR (pooled in)
Stellate_cell EPITHELIAL_MESENCHYMAL_TRANSITION -1.39 0.0650 1.42 0.035
Endothelial_cell INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE 1.57 0.0071 1.45 0.034
Cholangiocyte NOTCH_SIGNALING -1.15 0.3400 -1.13 0.370
Cholangiocyte WNT_BETA_CATENIN_SIGNALING 1.05 0.4300 1.05 0.440

One disagreement is entirely explained by the grouping. The paper reports collagen fibril organization up in stellate cells. Holding MASL out, the nearest Hallmark set is not significant; pooling MASL into the reference as they did, it becomes significantly up. The reason is visible in the composition data above: MASL donors carry an unusually quiescent stellate compartment (80% quiescent, against 42% in controls), so folding them into the reference lowers its fibrogenic baseline and widens the contrast. Both results are defensible; they answer slightly different questions, and the fibrogenesis signal is worth knowing is sensitive to that choice.

One disagreement is not. The paper reports the interferon-gamma response down in endothelial cells; here it is up, under both reference definitions. The leading edge is VCAM1, CD274, IDO1, FAS and IL18BP, which are interferon-inducible endothelial activation genes, and VCAM1 induction is consistent with the leukocyte recruitment implied by the abundance results. The direction is also coherent across the tissue: interferon-gamma response is up in the structural compartments and down in every immune population tested. The most likely source of the discrepancy is that Hallmark’s response signature is broad where the GO term is a narrower signalling set, compounded by cell-level versus donor-level differential expression. This is flagged rather than resolved.

Two of their findings are not reproduced. Notch and Wnt signalling in cholangiocytes are not significant here under either grouping. Cholangiocytes are the least powered cell type in this analysis, with the fewest donors clearing the pseudo-sample threshold, so this is weak evidence against their result. Their Notch claim also rests primarily on cell-cell interaction analysis, which is not attempted here.
